articles.title: Representing the Large‐Scale Atmospheric Response to Mesoscale SST Variability in Climate Models
articles.titleEn: Representing the Large‐Scale Atmospheric Response to Mesoscale SST Variability in Climate Models
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Climate models are commonly run at resolutions that do not represent mesoscale ocean dynamics and therefore lack the oceanic eddies and fronts that strongly influence atmosphere–ocean exchange. As a result, these models tend to underestimate the ocean's role in driving atmosphere–ocean interactions in western boundary current regions, with implications for simulated climate variability and change. Here, we investigate whether the effects of mesoscale sea surface temperature (SST) features (those associated with eddies and fronts) on large‐scale circulation can be represented in a standard resolution climate model. We develop a partially coupled “pacemaker” configuration of the Norwegian Earth System Model version 2 (NorESM2) that allows us to introduce mesoscale SST features from a high‐resolution (0.125) ocean in the standard coupled model grid (1 in both ocean and atmosphere). Focusing on the Kuroshio Current, this amplifies the ocean‐to‐atmosphere turbulent heat fluxes in the Kuroshio region, as expected, but also produces notable effects in the free troposphere. Even with a 1 atmosphere, mesoscale SST features induce a robust local strengthening of the North Pacific storm track at low levels and a poleward shift aloft. The results demonstrate that, although typical climate models cannot resolve mesoscale dynamics, there is clear potential to incorporate their effects. With the growing body of observational products for atmosphere‐ocean exchange, developing more realistic parameterizations of mesoscale‐driven SST variability to improve the types of climate models used for future projections appears promising.

articles.title: Simulating Near‐Surface Environments in Neighborhoods Using WRF‐LES: Case Study of an Urban Atmospheric Boundary Layer During a Heatwave Event
articles.titleEn: Simulating Near‐Surface Environments in Neighborhoods Using WRF‐LES: Case Study of an Urban Atmospheric Boundary Layer During a Heatwave Event
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: This study presents an in‐depth comparison of meteorological observations and simulations from a high‐resolution numerical weather model during an urban heatwave in Baltimore, MD. The simulations use a multi‐level nested approach to bridge the mesoscale and neighborhood‐scale environments and to incorporate high‐resolution static data sources to better represent the urban surface. The nested Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) runs use a planetary boundary layer (PBL) or large‐eddy simulation (LES) closure, depending on the horizontal grid spacing of each domain. Comparing simulation results with observations demonstrates the successful replication of a daytime convective boundary layer (CBL). Meanwhile, the results reveal several model biases that static‐data updates cannot correct. First, the simulated boundary layer is too warm, too dry, and too deep at midday. This overestimation of daytime CBL depth likely stems in part from overestimating surface sensible heat flux, partly attributable to misrepresenting urban vegetation. Secondly, for forecast‐relevant variables such as daytime 2‐m air temperature and humidity, no clear benefit is observed when the horizontal grid spacing is reduced below the typical kilometer scale. Simulated nighttime temperatures do benefit from both higher‐resolution static data and finer grid resolution, but still struggle to capture the level of spatial variability observed. Overall, decreasing horizontal grid spacing alone does not eliminate the WRF simulation biases reported here, similar to results in previous studies, nor does applying local high‐resolution static land surface data. Future work should focus on improving urban land surface models.

articles.title: Development and clinical validation of a multimodal AI framework to predict persistent fever during antibiotic therapy in hospitalized patients with cancer
articles.titleEn: Development and clinical validation of a multimodal AI framework to predict persistent fever during antibiotic therapy in hospitalized patients with cancer
articles.abstract: Among hospitalized cancer patients, persistent fever despite intravenous antibiotics often triggers treatment escalation and additional diagnostics. Earlier identification of patients at low risk for ongoing fever could support more selective decision-making. We developed and compared multimodal AI frameworks to predict persistent fever at the 48–72-hour reassessment window. Models integrated structured variables, time-series, notes, and chest imaging. Models were developed in a University Hospital Essen cohort and evaluated using holdout validation, two pooled regional hospitals, and MIMIC-IV ICU. A feature-level tabularized multimodal TabPFN model showed consistent discrimination, with AUC 0.84 (95% CI, 0.81–0.86) in cross-validation, 0.82 (95% CI, 0.77–0.87) in holdout validation, and 0.78 (95% CI, 0.74–0.81) in MIMIC-IV; other multimodal strategies showed comparable but more variable performance. Performance was primarily driven by temperature dynamics, while chest-radiograph imaging provided no incremental predictive value. In a clinician validation study, the multimodal model outperformed clinicians (Trial 1 balanced accuracy: 0.77 vs 0.60; Trial 2: 0.79 vs 0.57), while clinician balanced accuracy reached 0.71 (95% CI 0.67–0.75) in the AI-assisted condition, suggesting potential benefit of AI support. Overall, multimodal AI demonstrates potential to support 48-hour antibiotic reassessment and stewardship-oriented decision-making, although further prospective studies are needed.

articles.title: Disagreements in global urban growth projections amplify uncertainties in deforestation and carbon emissions
articles.titleEn: Disagreements in global urban growth projections amplify uncertainties in deforestation and carbon emissions
articles.abstract: Global urbanization is profoundly reshaping 21st-century land systems, yet its future trajectory remains highly uncertain. Existing projections exhibit divergent urban growth patterns even under identical socioeconomic scenarios. Here, by synthesizing six urban growth projections, we reveal substantial disagreements in the extent and location of urban growth by 2100. These disagreements are amplified by land-system feedbacks, driving cross-dataset variation in urban-induced deforestation (1.75–4.91 million km 2 ) through direct forest conversion and indirect cropland displacement, assuming lost production is compensated by cropland expansion elsewhere. The associated emissions exhibit an absolute range of 29 to 76 GtCO 2 by 2100. Across 100 countries, this range accounts for an average of 3% of unconditional Nationally Determined Contribution emission budgets, reaching 26% in specific countries. Our findings establish cross-dataset disagreement as an important source of uncertainty in land and climate assessments, highlighting the need for robust spatial planning across plausible urban futures.

articles.title: Disturbances and climate drive tree elevational shifts
articles.titleEn: Disturbances and climate drive tree elevational shifts
articles.abstract: Climate change and disturbances are reshaping forest ecosystems worldwide 1–4 , yet their combined effects on species redistribution remain poorly understood. Here we analyse repeated measurements from 44,368 forest inventory plots spanning 1999–2025, with an average remeasurement interval of 10 years, to examine how climate and natural disturbances jointly influence the elevational redistribution of tree species across the western USA. We show that climate warming increased sapling abundance, whereas increasing drought frequency and recent natural disturbances (fire, insect outbreaks and disease) reduced tree abundance, particularly among adult trees. By contrast, legacy fire was associated with increased sapling abundance, with stronger positive responses in angiosperms than in gymnosperms. These influences were distributed unevenly across species’ elevational ranges: upper portions of species’ ranges generally experienced stronger warming, greater increases in drought frequency and more disturbance activity than lower portions, creating elevational asymmetries in stress and recovery. These elevational asymmetries were associated with more pronounced downslope shifts in basal area centres, probably reflecting disturbance effects on larger trees. By contrast, stem abundance centres showed more divergent shifts, consistent with sapling responses to both climate change and disturbance. Our findings reveal contrasting demographic responses to climate change and natural disturbances that shape the elevational redistribution of different species, with potential consequences for forest composition, resilience and long-term stability.

articles.title: Design of ionic self-assembled monolayers suppressing proton release to mitigate proton-based degradation of perovskite solar cells
articles.titleEn: Design of ionic self-assembled monolayers suppressing proton release to mitigate proton-based degradation of perovskite solar cells
articles.abstract: Self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) serve as effective hole-transport layers (HTLs) in perovskite solar cells (PSCs), facilitating energy-level alignment and defect passivation at perovskite interfaces. However, their integration is limited by weak anchoring to transparent conducting oxides (TCOs), resulting in desorption during deposition and the release of acidic protons, which react with components of the perovskite leading to degradation [T. Li et al., Nature 648, 84–90 (2025) and C. Fei et al., Science 391, eadz7969 (2026)]. To strengthen anchoring between the SAM and TCO while simultaneously mitigating proton-induced degradation of the perovskite, we have prepared ionic SAMs featuring a phosphonate anchoring group and a perovskite-compatible cation. The benchmark SAMs, [2-(3,6-dimethoxy-9 H -carbazol-9-yl)ethyl]phosphonic acid (MeO-2PACz) for tin-based PSCs and [4-(3,6-dimethyl-9H-carbazol-9-yl)butyl]phosphonic acid (Me-4PACz) for lead-based PSCs, were reacted with formamidine, generated in situ via precipitation of KCl from formamidinium chloride (FACl) and KOH, to afford [FA] + [MeO-2PACz] − and [FA] + [Me-4PACz] − , respectively. After thermal aging at 65 °C in a N 2 atmosphere for 10 h, the [FA] + [MeO-2PACz] − -based device retained approximately 85% of its initial power conversion efficiency (PCE), compared with only 65% for the MeO-2PACz-based device, demonstrating enhanced thermal stability. Using [FA] + [Me-4PACz] − as the HTL in lead-based PSCs results in devices with a PCE of 26.53%, outperforming the PCE of 24.97% for the Me-4PACz-based device. After heating at 85°C for over 1,000 h, the [FA] + [Me-4PACz] − -based device retained ca. 88% of its initial efficiency. This study establishes the broad utility of ionic SAMs as versatile compounds to concurrently increase device efficiency and long-term stability.

articles.title: A deep-learning-boosted framework for quantum sensing with nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond
articles.titleEn: A deep-learning-boosted framework for quantum sensing with nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond
articles.abstract: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond are a versatile quantum sensing platform for high sensitivity measurements of magnetic fields, temperature, and strain with nanoscale spatial resolution. A common bottleneck is the analysis of optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) spectra, where target quantities are encoded in resonance features. Conventional nonlinear fitting is often computationally expensive, sensitive to initialization, and prone to failure at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Here we introduce a robust, efficient machine learning (ML) framework for real-time ODMR analysis based on a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN). The model performs direct parameter inference without initial guesses or iterative optimization, and is naturally parallelizable on graphics processing units (GPU) for high-throughput processing. We validate the approach on both synthetic and experimental datasets, showing improved throughput, accuracy, and robustness than standard nonlinear fitting, with the largest gains in the low-SNR regime. We further validate our methods in two representative sensing applications: diagnosing intracellular temperature changes using nanodiamond probes and widefield magnetic imaging of superconducting vortices in a high-temperature superconductor. This deep-learning inference framework enables fast and reliable extraction of physical parameters from complex ODMR data and provides a scalable route to real-time quantum sensing and imaging.

articles.title: Pyrethroid insecticide exposure enhances the ability of Helicoverpa armigera to counter host plant defenses through symbiotic bacteria
articles.titleEn: Pyrethroid insecticide exposure enhances the ability of Helicoverpa armigera to counter host plant defenses through symbiotic bacteria
articles.abstract: Like plant toxins, synthetic insecticides can exert strong selective pressures on pest populations. While responses to both plant toxins and synthetic insecticides can depend on adaptive changes in the nuclear genotype of the pest species, increasing evidence suggests that symbiotic microbes, particularly gut microbes, can also influence these responses. In the cotton bollworm, Helicoverpa armigera , concentrations of the symbiont Corynebacterium glyciniphilum increased in moth strains that were treated with the pyrethroid pesticide lambda-cyhalothrin (LCH), and they were also high in LCH-resistant strains and in populations exposed to 2-Tridecanone (2-TD), a secondary defense compound that is present in the Solanaceae. This increase enhanced the ability of H. armigera to overcome not only the pesticide but also a key defense mechanism in the solanaceous plants. In field populations of H. armigera , the abundance of C. glyciniphilum was lowest in populations feeding on nonsolanaceous plants that were sensitive to LCH. Based on gene knockouts, the underlying reason for the enhanced defensive capability provided by C. glyciniphilum was attributed to two detoxification enzyme genes (a P450 cytochrome and an esterase ) which can metabolize both LCH and 2-TD into nontoxic degradation products. These findings suggest that a common mechanism mediated by a symbiont contributes to the insect’s capacity to develop resistance to both a pesticide and a host plant toxin.

articles.title: Temperature-dependent kinetic isotope effects in methane reactions with OH and Cl reshape atmospheric sink fractionation
articles.titleEn: Temperature-dependent kinetic isotope effects in methane reactions with OH and Cl reshape atmospheric sink fractionation
articles.abstract: The abundances of stable isotopes in methane (CH 4 ) are used to distinguish fossil and biological emissions and to constrain the global methane budget. While these analyses require correction for isotopic fractionation occurring in methane’s atmospheric reactions, the temperature dependence of the kinetic isotope effects (KIEs) are poorly described and typically ignored. Here we combine density functional theory, Møller–Plesset perturbation theory, coupled-cluster calculations, and tunneling-corrected transition state theory to develop a first-principles description of the temperature-dependent KIEs for CH 4 and its isotopologues reacting with OH and Cl over the range 100 to 500 K which exhibit substantial and previously neglected temperature dependence. Incorporation of these KIEs into the EMAC chemistry–climate model yields systematically different effective atmospheric sink fractionation factors than those obtained using temperature-invariant values. The largest differences occur for chlorine oxidation in the cold upper troposphere and stratosphere, where methane isotope budgets are particularly sensitive to reactive halogens. We find a weak 13 C–D clumping anomaly and a strong D–D clumping anomaly, confirming earlier work and demonstrating that atmospheric oxidation produces substantial enrichment in Δ 12 CH 2 D 2 , and helping to reconcile source signatures with atmospheric observations. These results show that temperature-dependent KIEs are required for robust interpretation of methane isotopes in both contemporary and past atmospheres.

articles.title: Unlocking the unparalleled paleoclimate record of Antarctic blue ice areas
articles.titleEn: Unlocking the unparalleled paleoclimate record of Antarctic blue ice areas
articles.abstract: Ice uniquely provides direct samples of ancient atmosphere, enabling measurements of greenhouse gases contemporaneous to temperature reconstructions. Blue ice areas (covering 1% of the surface of Antarctica) hold a largely underexplored paleoclimate record that can extend beyond deep ice cores (that is, older than 1.5 My), covering periods in which global surface temperatures were similar to projected future temperatures. Blue ice areas expose ancient ice directly at the surface or at shallow depths due to net ablation and redirected ice flow, providing access to old ice at logistically reduced costs. However, the analysis and interpretation of blue ice samples is challenging, given the complex flow patterns in these regions that result in tilted layers, inversions and discontinuities in the stratigraphy, and complex ice–bedrock interactions. This paper presents a succinct review of state-of-the-art blue ice research, placed in the context of established ice core research, and argues that to advance the search for ancient ice, efforts in blue ice areas should focus on: i) collecting dated surface samples, ii) investigating the relationship between the age of the ice and other datable evidence, such as moraines, dust layers, meteorites, and exposed bedrock, and iii) developing models that can capture the typically disturbed or discontinuous stratigraphy. Together with advances in analytical techniques that address, for example, contamination and absolute dating, these efforts could lead to the recovery of the oldest ice on Earth, unravel warm climates of the past, and improve future climate change projections.

articles.title: A two-dimensional molecular gearbox operated in a crystalline solid
articles.titleEn: A two-dimensional molecular gearbox operated in a crystalline solid
articles.abstract: Since the earliest artificial gears, parallel gearbox systems based on intermeshing two-dimensional (2D) networks of multiple gear units have served a fundamental role in macroscale mechanical devices through the correlated mechanical motion of multiple gears. However, the realization of molecular-level 2D gearbox machinery with correlated motion among multiple units remains highly challenging. Here, we report a molecular-level 2D gearbox in a crystal, formed through the supramolecular assembly of an Au(I)-complex rotor with tripodal triptycene and triadamantyl phosphine (Ad 3 P) rotators, connected via an ethynyl–Au(I) unit. Upon heating, the rotators within a 2D hexagonal gear network exhibit 120° site-exchange rotational motion in a correlated manner, as revealed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction (XRD), 2 H solid-state (SS) NMR spectroscopy, and time-resolved variable-temperature XRD measurements. In addition, density functional theory calculations provide insight into the energetic preference for correlated motion within the gear-network. This 2D intermolecular gearbox in the crystalline state represents a supramolecular platform in which the intermolecular gearing motion has a large impact on the bulk crystal, which could provide a bridge between molecular-level mechanical properties and macroscale SS physical functions.

articles.title: Contrasting spatial homogeneity in atmospheric ice-nucleating particles from local to synoptic scales
articles.titleEn: Contrasting spatial homogeneity in atmospheric ice-nucleating particles from local to synoptic scales
articles.abstract: Ice-nucleating particles (INPs) play a critical role in regulating glaciation and precipitation formation in mixed-phase cloud (containing liquid and ice), yet their spatial variability across different scales remains poorly constrained. In this study, coordinated immersion freezing INP measurements from multiple sites during two campaigns in an urban–rural environment and complex mountainous terrain were used to investigate INP spatial distributions at tens-of-kilometer scales. At these scales, INP concentrations were generally spatially homogeneous during each campaign, indicating that single-site measurements can often represent surrounding areas. Occasional spatial differences were observed at warm activation temperatures (higher than −20 °C), ascribed to variations in heat-labile, likely biological INPs. Extending the analysis to the synoptic scale across multiple campaigns, warm-temperature INPs showed greater site-to-site differences, suggesting stronger influences from local or regional sources. In contrast, INPs active at colder temperatures showed much stronger spatial similarity between two inland continental sites separated by 800 km, revealing a broader regional coherence in this INP population. This was also observed at the coastal site, but only under continental air mass influence; the similarity weakened under marine air masses. These results suggest that cold-temperature INPs may reflect a broader INP background over continents such as that contributed by windblown dust. Our findings provide direct observational constraints on the representativeness of single-site INP measurements, which can help inform the strategy for representing variations in INP populations in atmospheric models.

articles.title: Modulating chain conformations and hydrogen-bond dynamics at silica–rubber interfaces for enhanced energy dissipation in composites
articles.titleEn: Modulating chain conformations and hydrogen-bond dynamics at silica–rubber interfaces for enhanced energy dissipation in composites
articles.abstract: The polymer–nanoparticle interphase is essential for fabricating high-performance nanocomposites, as it dictates mechanical properties through interfacial stress transfer and energy dissipation. However, engineering the buried interphases remains challenging due to the complex hierarchical structure and methodological limitations, particularly in silica–rubber systems where confined polymer chain conformation and hydrogen-bond dynamics are poorly resolved. Herein, a selective polymer-removal technique was developed to strip free and loosely bound polymer under extreme conditions, enabling TEM visualization of polymer chain-like interfacial features consistent with train-, loop-, and tail-like adsorption motifs in silica/silicone rubber nanocomposites. Correlative analysis combining STEM-EELS, high-resolution NMR, in situ variable-temperature IR, and 2D low-field NMR spectroscopy resolves hydrogen bonding between silica surface hydroxyls and silicone backbone oxygen atoms (Si-O-H···O-Si), which exhibit temperature-dependent behavior. Quantitative analysis reveals the strategic modulation of interphase layer thickness: As the apparent hydroxyl density of silica varied from 2.1 to 12.9 OH nm −2 , the interphase thickness increased from 4.1 ± 0.8 nm to 13.2 ± 1.4 nm (9.5 mol% polymer phenyl); increasing the polymer phenyl content to 29.7 mol% further expands the layer to 23.4 ± 1.0 nm. Molecular dynamics simulations also suggest that higher silica surface hydroxyl density enhances multipoint adsorption of polymer chain, which promotes the formation of loop and train conformations. These confined chain arrangements are consistent with the reduced Arrhenius activation energy from 101 to 50 kJ mol −1 measured by dynamic rheology, which facilitates interfacial chain mobility and hydrogen-bond exchange during deformation. These findings provide molecular-level insights for the rational design of polymer nanocomposites.

articles.title: A Depth‐Averaged Discontinuous Galerkin Morphodynamic Model With Orthogonal Bubble Function‐Based Boundary Treatment
articles.titleEn: A Depth‐Averaged Discontinuous Galerkin Morphodynamic Model With Orthogonal Bubble Function‐Based Boundary Treatment
articles.abstract: A discontinuous Galerkin (DG) model is developed for river morphodynamic simulations based on a depth‐averaged coupled shallow‐water–Exner formulation, in which the hydrodynamics are described by the shallow water equations, while the bedload transport rate is evaluated using the Wong–Parker bedload relation and the bed evolution is updated through the Exner equation. A Hasegawa‐type bedload‐direction correction is further introduced to represent the effects of curvature‐induced secondary flow and transverse bed slope on the direction of bedload transport. The model features an improved boundary treatment using orthogonal bubble function elements. The proposed framework utilizes linear triangular elements in the interior domain and specialized orthogonal bubble function elements along solid boundaries, enabling accurate and stable enforcement of the no‐normal‐flow condition. In addition, a nodal‐normal‐based treatment is introduced to ensure a smooth and continuous representation of solid boundaries. These boundary treatments provide robust numerical solutions for sediment transport processes near riverbanks. Benchmark tests, laboratory validation cases, and a field‐scale application demonstrate mesh‐ and time‐step‐convergent solutions, reasonable agreement with measured bed deformation, and stable computation over a realistic river geometry. The results also show that including the Hasegawa‐type correction can improve the predicted erosion–deposition patterns in curved channels. The results indicate that the proposed DG framework provides a promising and robust basis for coupled hydrodynamic–morphodynamic simulations in riverine settings and can be further extended to more complex hydro‐morphodynamic processes.

articles.title: Assessing the Added Value of Earth Observations for Multi‐Model Kilometer‐Scale Hydrological Modeling Across Contrasting Basins
articles.titleEn: Assessing the Added Value of Earth Observations for Multi‐Model Kilometer‐Scale Hydrological Modeling Across Contrasting Basins
articles.abstract: Earth observation (EO) products provide spatially and temporally detailed information on key water‐cycle processes, yet their value for improving hydrological and land‐surface model simulations remains uncertain. Here, we evaluate high‐resolution EO data for daily streamflow simulations at 1 km resolution across contrasting hydroclimatic and data‐density regimes in Europe and Africa, using up to five model structures (five in the Po, four in the Rhine and three in the Tugela). We explore two complementary pathways: (a) replacing conventional meteorological forcing with EO‐based precipitation, and (b) estimating model parameters with EO constraints on soil moisture, evapotranspiration, and snow cover, either alone or jointly with streamflow. Model skill is quantified using the Kling–Gupta Efficiency (KGE) and its components, based on paired gauge comparisons. Results show that EO precipitation forcing improves streamflow simulations in the Po and Tugela river basins, but reduces skill in the Rhine. Calibration against EO variables alone yields mixed outcomes, whereas joint calibration with EO variables and streamflow, available for three of the models, gives more consistent improvements, particularly for TETIS in the Tugela and mHM in the Po. KGE decomposition reveals that improved variability alignment is the dominant contributor to these gains, with changes in bias and timing playing secondary roles. Despite differences across models and basins, our findings show that EO integration can enhance kilometer‐scale hydrological simulations in specific model–basin configurations, particularly when combined with discharge information. This highlights both the potential and the current limits of available EO products as complementary constraints for operational hydrology, flood and drought early warning, and climate‐resilient water management.

We explore two complementary pathways: (a) replacing conventional meteorological forcing with EO‐based precipitation, and (b) estimating model parameters with EO constraints on soil moisture, evapotranspiration, and snow cover, either alone or jointly with streamflow. Model skill is quantified using the Kling–Gupta Efficiency (KGE) and its components, based on paired gauge comparisons. Results show that EO precipitation forcing improves streamflow simulations in the Po and Tugela river basins, but reduces skill in the Rhine. Calibration against EO variables alone yields mixed outcomes, whereas joint calibration with EO variables and streamflow, available for three of the models, gives more consistent improvements, particularly for TETIS in the Tugela and mHM in the Po. KGE decomposition reveals that improved variability alignment is the dominant contributor to these gains, with changes in bias and timing playing secondary roles. Despite differences across models and basins, our findings show that EO integration can enhance kilometer‐scale hydrological simulations in specific model–basin configurations, particularly when combined with discharge information. This highlights both the potential and the current limits of available EO products as complementary constraints for operational hydrology, flood and drought early warning, and climate‐resilient water management.

articles.title: Climate change intensifies hydrological seasonality in Denmark: Insights from an integrated model assessment
articles.titleEn: Climate change intensifies hydrological seasonality in Denmark: Insights from an integrated model assessment
articles.abstract: Temperate regions across Europe, such as Denmark, are projected to be subject to substantial changes in the hydrological cycle due to climate change. Changes in climate can materialize as general changes in long term means, extremes, or in seasonal patterns, e.g., dampening or intensification of the seasonal contrasts. Changes in seasonal patterns can affect the hydrological cycle in various ways, due to the interlinkage between hydrological compartments. To detect, track and quantify the impact of changes in climate and seasonal patterns, integrated hydrological modelling is needed. This makes Denmark an ideal test case due to the established integrated and physically based National Hydrological Model of Denmark (DK-model). Utilizing climate projections from 17 regional climate models under the high-emission scenario RCP8.5, downscaled and bias-corrected for Denmark, we calculate climate change impacts on both overall values and seasonality for the variables soil moisture, streamflow, shallow and deeper groundwater to the middle and end of the century. Moreover, standardized hydrological drought indices are calculated for the same variables. Climate change projections point towards a future with higher annual precipitation, mainly due to wetter winters, while climatic water balance deficits increase during summer; thus, intensifying the seasonal contrast. The increased contrast is reappearing in the fast-responding hydrological variable, soil moisture; while streamflow and shallow groundwater clearly reproduce increase during the wetter winter, the summer signal differs. The deep groundwater systems experience higher future groundwater heads across the entire year. Common for all variables is a larger seasonality, defined as contrast between intra-annual low and highs. Notably, the ensemble of hydrological projections is more in agreement regarding the seasonal contrast than on the direction of absolute change, with results agreeing for 55 % to 99 % of the area of Denmark on increased seasonality, whereas only agreeing for 12 % to 72 % on the absolute direction of that change. The drought indices exhibit a similar seasonal change, with more droughts during summer and more wet anomalies during winter for soil moisture, while summer droughts for streamflow and shallow groundwater partially are buffered by wetter winters and the related recharge increase. In summary, the results indicate that despite considerable increases in precipitation, projected climate change for Denmark is expected to enhance hydrological seasonality instead of producing a uniform transition to a wetter regime, potentially impacting the climate adaptation and mitigation effort, agricultural yields, and water supply.

articles.title: Compression Safeguards: building trust into lossy data compression
articles.titleEn: Compression Safeguards: building trust into lossy data compression
articles.abstract: The growth in data volumes produced by scientific models is accelerating. Data production of high-resolution weather and climate models is outpacing the methods and budgets for storing, sharing, and analysing this data, posing a threat to scientific progress. Lossy data compression greatly reduces data sizes but loses some quality, detail, or precision of the original data. Even though some lossy compressors promise size reductions of 100× or more, the lack of trust in lossy compression, rooted in the risk of losing important information, has thus far limited their adoption. We introduce Compression Safeguards , a user-centric and domain-independent framework to overcome this trust gap, with which (i) scientists declare their precise safety requirements for what lossy compression must preserve, e.g. regionally varying error bounds on quantities derived from the decompressed data, then (ii) wrap a compressor of their choice in the corresponding safeguards, which then (iii) guarantee that the user-declared safety requirements are always met by the safeguarded compressor. The Compression Safeguards represent a paradigm shift: Data producers and users no longer carry the risks of lossy compression, having to manually check for problems after compression, but instead control up-front what needs to be safeguarded. With the appropriate application-specific safeguards, trust can grow in all lossy compressors and even untrusted, potentially unsafe compressors can be used safely and with confidence. Users thus no longer need to re-verify each new compressor for each new use case, or to restrict themselves to few safe compressors and supported use cases. We showcase how our reference implementation of the Compression Safeguards can be flexibly applied to safeguard important properties across several real-world examples from weather and climate sciences for different compressors. The cost of the Safeguards is a reduced compression throughput, significantly when safeguarding complex safety requirements, and lower compression ratios if the Safeguards have to correct the decompressed data to uphold its safety. There is only minor overhead during decompression. Altogether, Compression Safeguards provide a key modular tool that gives users the confidence to use lossy compression safely across scientific disciplines. Safeguards can unlock the data reduction benefits of lossy compression and therefore solve many data storage problems across the scientific community that otherwise hinder research.

articles.title: GEOS-Chem-hyd: enabling source-oriented sensitivity analysis with GEOS-Chem
articles.titleEn: GEOS-Chem-hyd: enabling source-oriented sensitivity analysis with GEOS-Chem
articles.abstract: Effective environmental policymaking requires accurate quantification of how changes in emissions impact air quality. Chemical transport models, such as GEOS-Chem, are widely used for such analysis. Traditional methods to compute the relative influence of a change in emissions, or the sensitivity of pollutant concentrations to a change in emissions, with these models often suffer from numerical inaccuracies, especially when evaluating nonlinear atmospheric processes. To overcome these limitations, we integrated a novel sensitivity analysis approach leveraging hyperdual numbers into GEOS-Chem, making GEOS-Chem-hyd. The hyperdual step method accurately calculates first- and second-order sensitivities simultaneously and avoids common numerical errors associated with traditional finite difference methods. The real concentrations as well as first- and second-order sensitivities with respect to emissions calculated with GEOS-Chem-hyd align with the values calculated with GEOS-Chem version 14.0.0-rc.3 within expected error. GEOS-Chem-hyd is applied to assess how changes in emissions of nitrogen oxides can alter ozone, particulate matter, ammonium, and biogenic organic aerosol concentrations, demonstrating regional differences and nonlinear influences. As an example of regional variations, the relative influence of increasing nitrogen oxide emissions was to decrease biogenic organic aerosol concentrations in most areas, except in portions of the boreal forests in Siberia. The nonlinear influence of emissions of nitrogen oxides on ozone, ammonium, and biogenic organic aerosol was evidenced by second-order sensitivities on the same order of magnitude as the first-order sensitivities. GEOS-Chem-hyd incurs approximately four times greater computational costs than GEOS-Chem, which is competitive with the three GEOS-Chem model executions required for less accurate second-order sensitivities using the central finite difference method. GEOS-Chem-hyd provides a framework for efficient assessment of the influence of new scientific modules, which are easily incorporated into the sensitivity analysis framework, and supports informed emission control policy development through accurate, source-oriented sensitivity analysis.

articles.title: Overview of ParallelClim-WestUS-Daily – high-resolution observed and counterfactual daily climate data for the western United States, 1951–2025
articles.titleEn: Overview of ParallelClim-WestUS-Daily – high-resolution observed and counterfactual daily climate data for the western United States, 1951–2025
articles.abstract: Extreme climate events and trends commonly elicit curiosity as to the role of anthropogenic climate change. In the western United States (US), severe droughts and heatwaves over the first quarter of the 21st century have strained water-management, agricultural, and ecological systems while also putting humans at risk from wildfires and hydrological hazards. Understanding whether and how climate change has promoted or intensified these processes requires estimating anthropogenic effects on a wide range of climate variables, including background mean conditions, higher-frequency variances, and how these changes have been distributed intra-annually and spatially. Here we introduce ParallelClim-WestUS-Daily, a new dataset of observed daily, high-resolution (∼ 4 km) gridded climate data for the western US from 1951–2025 as well as a parallel, counterfactual realization of the observed sequence of climate but excluding anthropogenic changes in background mean climate and daily variances. Our dataset includes eight surface variables commonly used in hydrological, vegetation, and wildfire modeling: daily precipitation total, daily maximum and minimum temperature, and daily means of vapor pressure, wind speed, downwelling shortwave and longwave radiation, and surface pressure. Anthropogenic climate change is estimated as the weighted mean change among 24 climate models relative to the second half of the 19th century according to the CMIP6 Historical experiment through 2014, extended with SSP2-4.5 for 2015–2025. Model weightings are based on agreement with global surface temperature trends, limiting the influence of models with likely unrealistic climate sensitivities to greenhouse-gas forcing. The ParallelClim-WestUS-Daily dataset will allow new opportunities to explore effects of anthropogenic climate change on western US hydroclimate and complex hydroclimatic impacts such as soil moisture, snowpack, streamflow, vegetation productivity, and wildfire. The ParallelClim-WestUS-Daily dataset is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19636838 (Williams, 2026c) for the observed climate and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20261472 (Williams, 2026b) for the counterfactual climate.

articles.title: GIFT-BDS: a high-resolution TEC and Gradient Ionospheric Index dataset over China derived from BeiDou GEO fixed-geometry observations
articles.titleEn: GIFT-BDS: a high-resolution TEC and Gradient Ionospheric Index dataset over China derived from BeiDou GEO fixed-geometry observations
articles.abstract: High-resolution ionospheric total electron content (TEC) gradient observations are well-suited for characterizing ionospheric spatial structure and for assessing ionospheric effects on Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) positioning applications. Existing global ionospheric products provide valuable information on large-scale ionospheric conditions, but their spatial and temporal sampling is generally not sufficient to resolve fine-scale TEC gradient structures over China. We present GIFT-BDS (Gradient Ionospheric index from Fixed-geometry TEC observations using BDS GEO satellites), a high-resolution regional ionospheric dataset derived from a dense ground-based GNSS network and BeiDou geostationary Earth orbit (GEO) fixed-geometry observations. The network consists of more than 200 ground-based GNSS receivers and five BeiDou GEO satellites, providing stable receiver-satellite geometries and repeated sampling of nearly fixed ionospheric pierce points. The released dataset contains two product levels. Level-1 provides 30 s GEO-derived slant TEC (STEC) time series for individual receiver-satellite links. Level-2 provides gridded vertical TEC (VTEC), rate of TEC index (ROTI), Gradient Ionospheric Index (GIX), and directional TEC gradient components. The TEC-gradient products are provided on a 0.25° × 0.25° grid with a temporal resolution of 15 min. The dataset is assessed using STEC stability statistics, internal consistency diagnostics, and comparison with Global Ionospheric Map (GIM)-derived gradients. Selected examples illustrate the use of GIFT-BDS for studies of daytime Equatorial Ionization Anomaly (EIA) morphology, nighttime Equatorial Plasma Bubble (EPB) evolution, and ionospheric effects on Precise Point Positioning (PPP) and Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) positioning performance. The dataset is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21090695 (Li et al., 2026a), with operational updates provided at https://data.bdsmart.cn/pub/campaign/iono/ (last access: 23 November 2026). GIFT-BDS extends the currently available ionospheric data resources over China by providing continuous high-resolution observations of TEC and TEC gradients, enabling investigations of ionospheric dynamics, space-weather effects, and GNSS positioning error characterization.

articles.title: Developing a spatially distributed typical meteorological year dataset for solar radiation assessment in Australia
articles.titleEn: Developing a spatially distributed typical meteorological year dataset for solar radiation assessment in Australia
articles.abstract: Spatially distributed Typical Meteorological Year (TMY) products are important for solar-radiation evaluation and building-performance simulations, particularly in regions where conventional station-based TMY products have limited spatial coverage and delayed updates. This study develops TMY-MER, a recent-period MERRA2-based typical-year product for GHI-centered solar-radiation evaluation across Australia. Hourly MERRA2 data from 2009 to 2023 were used to construct typical-year weather files for 353 representative city-coordinate or local-government-area locations. A weather-type-conditioned GHI discrepancy assessment framework was introduced to distinguish clear-sky and overcast conditions. Weather-type-conditioned GHI bias parameters were derived by comparing TMY-MER with a reference TMY product at 122 comparison locations and were spatially interpolated using inverse distance weighting (IDW) to generate TMY-MER-IDW. The quantitative assessment focuses on GHI discrepancies rather than full multi-variable validation, while non-GHI variables are retained from MERRA2 as contextual variables for weather-file construction. The results show that TMY-MER exhibits relatively small GHI discrepancies under clear-sky conditions, generally within 5 % on an annual basis, whereas overcast conditions show larger deviations, with maximum discrepancies reaching approximately 40 % due to uncertainties in cloud and aerosol representation. DIRINT-based decomposition and Ladybug Tools building-cluster simulations were further conducted as application-oriented analyses to examine downstream usability and simulation consistency. The resulting TMY-MER and TMY-MER-IDW products provide a spatially distributed basis for GHI-centered solar-radiation analysis and building-scale solar-radiation applications across Australia. The TMY-MER-IDW dataset is publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15479502 (Fu et al., 2025).

articles.title: Gross primary productivity of forest ecosystems in a subtropical city and its decadal climatic and environmental drivers
articles.titleEn: Gross primary productivity of forest ecosystems in a subtropical city and its decadal climatic and environmental drivers
articles.abstract: Vegetation plays a vital role in modulating climate and the carbon cycle on land through processes like photosynthesis, also known as gross primary production (GPP). The significant presence of vegetation in Hong Kong, covering over 70 % of the land area, highlights the potential for terrestrial carbon sink to contribute to achieving carbon neutrality in such a metropolitan city. Meanwhile, the terrestrial ecosystem is also influenced by climatic and environmental factors. This study investigates the historical spatiotemporal dynamics of GPP in the subtropical forests of Hong Kong and the key drivers behind its trend and interannual variability between 2002 and 2018. We used the Terrestrial Ecosystem Model in R-Hong Kong (TEMIR-HK), a localized process-based ecophysiological model, to evaluate the changes in GPP induced by changing CO 2 concentration, temperature, ozone (O 3 ) concentration, and changing leaf area index (LAI) shaped by these factors as well as land use. Simulation results indicate an increasing trend of GPP, with an average annual GPP of 1.75 TgC yr −1 , which is around 15 % of the annual total anthropogenic carbon emission from Hong Kong, suggesting a limited but indispensable potential of forestry to achieve city-level carbon neutrality. Model simulations of GPP show satisfactory results when spatially comparing with satellite-derived GPP dataset ( R =0.89), with slight difference of +8.7 % on average. Factorial simulations reveal LAI changes dominate both trend (+0.0134 TgC yr −2 ) and interannual variability (2.77 × 10 −2 TgC yr −1 ) of GPP in Hong Kong. This result highlights that local-scale reforestation could influence GPP trend over the whole city and emphasizes the importance on the accuracy of LAI input in ecosystem-scale photosynthesis modelling. This work contributes to improving the scientific understanding on subtropical forest ecosystems, and highlights the potential, though limited, of Hong Kong forests to play their parts in working toward carbon neutrality targets.

articles.title: Improved estimation of extreme sea levels via non-asymptotic statistical methods for coastal hazard assessment
articles.titleEn: Improved estimation of extreme sea levels via non-asymptotic statistical methods for coastal hazard assessment
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Because sea level records are often short, non-asymptotic extreme value modeling is more accurate, as it does not depend on large-sample limiting assumptions. However, selecting independent events (IEs) is critical and depends on the chosen sea level threshold (SLT) and time window width (TWW) used. Existing literature often lacks a definitive methodology for IE selection. This study aimed to fill this gap by proposing two methodologies for selecting IEs (overlapping and sorting approaches) and a methodology to find the optimal combination of TWW and SLT. The identified IEs were employed to model extreme sea level events utilizing the Peak Over Threshold-Generalized Pareto Distribution (POT-GPD) and the metastatistical extreme value distribution (MEVD) approaches. A cross-validation approach, along with statistical metrics, was used to rigorously assess performance. Findings indicate that MEVD outperforms POT-GPD and is effective in estimating extreme events with longer return periods (RPs). Overall, MEVD with the overlapping method proved more effective at predicting long RP events, although MEVD with the sorting approach had comparatively lower uncertainty.

articles.title: Modelling firebrand dynamics in a coupled Fire-Atmosphere models: an Eulerian approach
articles.titleEn: Modelling firebrand dynamics in a coupled Fire-Atmosphere models: an Eulerian approach
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Spotting, the process by which burning firebrands are lifted by convection and transported downwind igniting secondary fires, can become a critical driver of rapid wildfire spread and presents major challenges for prediction and suppression. Coupled Fire-Atmosphere models, which simulate the two-way interaction between fire behaviour and local atmospheric dynamics, offer a promising avenue to capture such complex processes. In this study, we introduce a computationally efficient Eulerian formulation for firebrand transport, implemented within the coupled MesoNH–ForeFire modelling framework. Two case studies were analysed: an idealized scenario over flat and hilly terrain to assess orography influence, and a realistic simulation of the 2016 Mt Bolton wildfire in southeastern Australia. Results demonstrate that this simplified approach provides a credible and time-efficient firebrand deposition forecast.

articles.title: Methodological framework for tsunami risk assessment in port facilities
articles.titleEn: Methodological framework for tsunami risk assessment in port facilities
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Although tsunami hazard modeling has advanced significantly, the development of asset-specific vulnerability functions and risk indicators at the terminal scale remains a critical challenge, hindering the effective integration of scientific knowledge into port infrastructure planning and risk management. The main objective of this study is to propose a methodological framework specifically tailored to tsunami risk assessment in port terminals. The analysis focuses on assessing damage to key components of the port supply chain located within the port's landside operational area and directly exposed to tsunami impacts. The proposed framework integrates advanced numerical hydrodynamic modeling, dynamic exposure analyses and asset-specific damage states. Its main novelty lies in the quantification of vulnerability thresholds based on hydrodynamic failure mechanisms for heterogeneous port assets, including container stacks, gantry cranes, liquid bulk tanks, roll-on/roll-off (Ro-Ro) cargo, and pedestrians. The methodology was applied to the Port of Cádiz, Spain. The results show that relative tsunami risk is spatially concentrated in specific operational areas and assets, particularly container storage yards and passenger circulation zones. The proposed framework is modular and can be adapted to other port contexts, provided that suitable local hazard, exposure, and asset information is available. Rather than providing absolute estimates of losses, the framework offers a spatially explicit decision-support basis for identifying critical assets, comparing relative risk among docks, and prioritising further detailed assessments or mitigation actions.

articles.title: National-scale debris-flow hazard indication modelling for Swiss railway infrastructure
articles.titleEn: National-scale debris-flow hazard indication modelling for Swiss railway infrastructure
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Debris flows are among the most destructive alpine hazards, threatening settlements and critical infrastructure with average annual damages in Switzerland of CHF 321 million. Hazard indication modelling of debris flows, among other hazards, offers the possibility to identify hazard hot spots at a regional and national scale. Additionally it lays the foundation for future scenario modelling. We present the Large-Scale Hazard Indication Modelling (LSHIM) framework for debris flows as commissioned by the Swiss federal railway (SBB) with guiding value return periods of 30, 100, and 300 years. For susceptibility modelling, we combine high-resolution digital terrain models, climatic and geologic layers, and statistical modelling with a random forest approach. Susceptibility is cross-validated against the Swiss event database (StorMe) with an average accuracy of 81.4 % and application results in 16 756 possible release areas. Dynamic runout is calculated with a tailored version of RAMMS::Debrisflow, where we define hydrograph volume from MeteoSchweiz-modelled extreme precipitation. Landscape erosivity is assessed by geology and geomorphology. Results indicate 55, 76, and 85 km of railway affected by debris flow hazard for a 30-, 100-, and 300-year return period, respectively. The highest intensity class shows the highest relative increase under longer return periods. This approach enables a large-scale hazard indication assessment based on high-quality input data. The results are a valuable base for further planning and investigations that incorporate climate change. Limitations in the methodology lie in the static definition of release area and deterministic parameterization.

articles.title: Detection of agricultural flash droughts using impact-informed thresholds
articles.titleEn: Detection of agricultural flash droughts using impact-informed thresholds
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Rapid and sustained evaporative stress can cause soils to lose moisture within days to weeks. When this rapid soil moisture depletion occurs during sensitive crop stages, it severely affects agricultural systems and manifests as agricultural flash droughts (AFDs). AFDs are often detected using fixed thresholds reported in the literature that assume uniformity across time and space, while rarely being linked to actual observed crop losses. However, this may poorly represent their occurrence and impacts in local contexts, thereby limiting their usefulness for decision-makers who require context-specific information. This study aims to overcome these limitations by introducing an impact-informed calibration of the Standardized Evaporative Stress Ratio (SESR) thresholds and linking them to observed crop losses. Thresholds are derived temporally across crop management periods and spatially across soil textures. The calibration is tested in the Central American Dry Corridor in Nicaragua, where rainfed agriculture predominates. Results suggest that evaporative stress signals differed between years with and years without drought-induced crop losses, with the clearest separation occurring during the crop-sensitive growing period in clayey soil textures. Results further show that, for these soils and during this period, calibrated thresholds provide a favourable balance between detecting years with drought-induced crop losses and reducing false alarms when compared with literature-based thresholds, whereas performance remains similarly low in sandy soils. Calibrated thresholds were considered skilful when they achieve high precision, high discrimination, and low uncertainty, and were identified during the pre-sowing and growing periods in moderately fine clay-loam and very fine expansive clayey soils. In loamy-silty soils, skilful thresholds were mainly observed during the pre-sowing period but not thereafter. Validation further shows that applying these skilful thresholds increases the detection of flash drought events associated with crop losses, with consistently higher hit rates than the literature-based thresholds. These findings indicate that monitoring AFDs using tailored, impact-informed thresholds has operational value for drought management and supports context-specific decision-making.

articles.title: Health impacts of urban water network upgrades from the PAASIM matched cohort trial in Beira, Mozambique
articles.titleEn: Health impacts of urban water network upgrades from the PAASIM matched cohort trial in Beira, Mozambique
articles.abstract: We conducted a matched-control study to assess the impact of substantial improvements to the urban water system in Beira, Mozambique, on child health and enteric infections. The intervention reduced overall infection with individual pathogens by 10% and co-infection by 13%, especially among children with more than two pathogens. However, we found no impact of the intervention on infection with bacteria or protozoa as classes of pathogens, nor on diarrhoea, child growth or child mortality outcomes. We found no association between direct household water connections—independent of intervention status—on any outcomes. Our evidence points to potential impacts of the intervention on enteric pathogen infections, but estimates were imprecise. The impact of the intervention may have been limited by the lack of provision of continuous, reliable water supply and lack of safe water storage, leading to household contamination and infection from non-water-supply routes of exposure.

articles.title: Source‐Sink Structures Shape Global Drought Propagation
articles.titleEn: Source‐Sink Structures Shape Global Drought Propagation
articles.abstract: The spatial propagation of drought plays a critical role in shaping synchronized global drought occurrences. As hubs (sources and sinks) for drought propagation, the global role of sources and sinks has not been thoroughly assessed. Identifying key propagation hotspots and tracing their global pathways is essential for understanding how droughts evolve over time and space. Here, five paired drought source (location that droughts move from)‐sink (region where droughts are more likely to propagate to) systems at the continental scale are identified: western Congo Basin‐eastern Congo Basin, Sahel and savanna regions‐Sahara Desert, Labrador Peninsula‐Great Plains, Amazon Plain‐Brazilian Plateau, Tarim Basin and Tianshan Mountain‐Central Siberian Plateau, Stanovoy Range, Yangtze River Basin, Middle East. Analyzing water vapor budget between sources and sinks reveals a pattern of drought propagation from sources to sinks, contrasting with water vapor moving in the opposite path. This exacerbates drought severity in drought sinks, a trend likely to intensify under future scenarios with increased radiative forcing. This study identifies a drought source‐sink structure, providing a new perspective on large‐scale drought spatial propagation. These offer critical insights for drought early warning and mitigation strategies across regions.

articles.title: Improving Turbulence Closure for Predicting Surface Signatures and Near‐Surface Mixing in Open Channel Flow
articles.titleEn: Improving Turbulence Closure for Predicting Surface Signatures and Near‐Surface Mixing in Open Channel Flow
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Patterns at the water surface can indicate turbulent underwater dynamics and their properties. We seek to connect the statistical predictions of second moment closure (SMC) models for time and length scales of subsurface turbulent structures linked to these observable free surface signatures. To isolate and motivate changes to SMC assumptions that undermine relevance to surface flow, we focus on the unforced free surface of a tidally driven estuary, idealized as open channel flow (OCF) with bottom shear turbulence production. We modify the traditional “return‐to‐isotropy” closure assumption for turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) components so that, in the absence of local production, near‐surface TKE anisotropy decays to a non‐zero depth‐dependent profile. In a modified weak‐equilibrium k – ε SMC model, combining prognostic equations for TKE ( k ) and dissipation ( ε ), this gives rise to distinct vertical and horizontal length scales at the surface, formed from TKE components and the dissipation timescale. The derived modification of vertical diffusivity is very similar to ad‐hoc near‐surface damping proposed by Nakayama and Yokojima (2003, https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1021136912983 ) to address excessive model flux predictions. An attendant increase in near‐surface horizontal diffusivities also resolves longstanding discrepancies for predicting transverse diffusion in shear dispersion experiments. Modified SMC predictions for TKE components, dissipation, and horizontal length scales at the free surface are compared with observations in a tidally driven estuary and with published OCF lab experiments and numerical simulations. Applicability of model improvements reported here appears limited to flows without vertical TKE production adjacent to the free surface.

articles.title: Carbon-neutral algal bloom management via algal organic matter repurposing
articles.titleEn: Carbon-neutral algal bloom management via algal organic matter repurposing
articles.abstract: Algal organic matter (AOM) has been considered a typical pollutant in algal bloom waters, conventionally managed through flocculation-flotation processes with high carbon footprints. This study presents a paradigm shift by redefining AOM as a functional crosslinker and developing an AOM-induced self-driven flotation (A-SDF) strategy. The approach utilizes active groups in AOM (-COOH/-OH) coordinated with trace amounts of metal coagulants to construct multilevel gel flocs with Al 2 O 3 /FeO(OH) crystalline phases. Remarkably, these flocs not only capture algal cells but also activate dissolved oxygen (DO), inducing DO enrichment-interfacial gas nucleation behavior (DOE-IGNB) and leading to microbubbles (MBs) formation at the floc interface under mild turbulence. The process achieved efficient removal of algal cells (82–95%), turbidity (86–95%), and AOM (45–79%) within 2 min without external aeration. Compared with existing technologies, the carbon footprint, treatment time, and economic cost were reduced by 66.08–96.90%, 71.67–96.00%, and 50.55–97.67%, respectively, while residual metal concentrations remained well below drinking water standards. Density functional theory calculations confirmed strong DO adsorption by tetrahedral AlO 4 /FeO 4 lattices as the molecular mechanism driving DOE-IGNB. By repurposing AOM as a resource and activating endogenous DO, this work provides a universal carbon-neutral pathway for sustainable algal bloom management worldwide.

articles.title: Excited-state twisted intramolecular charge transfer enables reversible light control of rhodamine-graphene binding
articles.titleEn: Excited-state twisted intramolecular charge transfer enables reversible light control of rhodamine-graphene binding
articles.abstract: Reversible light control of supramolecular interactions underpins fundamental processes in nature, inspiring artificial molecular devices and adaptive materials. Existing approaches rely on light-modulated interconversion between ground-state species characterized by distinct binding properties. Here, we introduce twisted intramolecular charge transfer (TICT) as an excited-state specific lever to modulate dye–surface adhesion. Using rhodamine B base (Rhb) as the photoactive species, we combine femtosecond spectroscopy with theoretical calculations to provide a direct observation of TICT formation and its thermal equilibrium with the locally excited state. We show that the associated dihedral twisting and charge redistribution weaken Rhb-graphene binding, enabling light-induced dye desorption in water. Molecular dynamics simulations corroborate that the out-of-plane TICT conformations induce steric hindrance against the graphene basal plane, significantly reducing the binding affinity and lowering the thermodynamic barrier of the dye-surface desorption. This synergy between experiment and theory establishes excited-state conformational dynamics as a general strategy to control supramolecular interactions in host-guest systems in physiological conditions, with implications for sensing, delivery, and materials science.

articles.title: Preventing data leakage in neural decoding
articles.titleEn: Preventing data leakage in neural decoding
articles.abstract: Neural decoding is a widely-used machine learning technique for investigating how behavior, perception and cognition are represented in neural activity. However without careful application data leakage can occur, where information from the test set contaminates the training set, leading to biased estimates of decoding performance and potentially invalidating biological conclusions. Here we show that leakage can be introduced in neural decoding studies by common supervised and unsupervised preprocessing steps, including dimensionality reduction. We reveal that in some cases leakage can paradoxically decrease decoding performance relative to unbiased estimates, and we provide theoretical analyses explaining how this occurs. We also show that, for autocorrelated neural time series, randomized k-fold cross-validation can dramatically overstate decoding performance. Based on these findings, we provide detailed recommendations for avoiding data leakage in neural decoding.

articles.title: Achieving high-yield and pilot-scale synthesis of nano graphene oxide via photochemical defect engineering and oxidative cleavage
articles.titleEn: Achieving high-yield and pilot-scale synthesis of nano graphene oxide via photochemical defect engineering and oxidative cleavage
articles.abstract: The high-yield synthesis of nanoscale graphene oxide is increasingly critical, yet widespread scalable implementation of top-down methods remains hindered by low efficiency. Here, we report a highly efficient, scaled-up approach coupling photochemical defect engineering and oxidative cleavage to fragment micron-sized graphene oxide into nanoscale flakes. Irradiation induces nanoscale holes on the graphene oxide basal plane, causing rapid fragmentation upon hydrogen peroxide treatment. This yields nanoscale graphene oxide (20 to 60 nanometers) featuring an sp 2 -hybridized carbon core and carboxylic acid-rich edges. The material exhibits exceptional stability against thermal ripening, prolonged solar irradiation, and chemical reduction. Achieving an 85 ± 5 % conversion yield, the practical scalability of this process is demonstrated using a pilot-scale device with a projected annual capacity of 0.52 tons of powder. This work provides a route for the pilot-scale production of high-performance nanoscale graphene oxide materials.

articles.title: LESSONS report: Fine-scale representation of consecutive dry days
articles.titleEn: LESSONS report: Fine-scale representation of consecutive dry days
articles.abstract: The number of consecutive dry days (CDD) is a widely used metric for assessing meteorological drought. This study investigates spatial CDD patterns over Germany during the drought year of 2018, comparing a convection-permitting model (CPM) at 3 km resolution with ERA5 reanalysis at 31 km, gauge-based interpolated observations at 1 km, and radar measurements at 1 km. The analysis reveals a surprise : high-resolution CPM and radar data produce strikingly heterogeneous, “brushstroke-like” spatial structures that differ fundamentally from the smooth fields of reanalysis and gridded observations. Our report confirms that these sharp spatial discontinuities are not computational artifacts but a physical consequence of the sensitivity to the fixed daily dryness threshold of the CDD metric. We find that the CPM can well reproduce these fine-scale patterns that are also detected by radar measurements, which is quantified by a spatial autocorrelogram and the radially averaged power spectral density. While averaging CDD over multiple years smooths out the brushstroke patterns, such temporal averaging does not resolve the underlying shortcoming : multi-year CDD is built upon individual annual CDD values that are, as shown here, highly variable and strongly dataset-dependent. A statistic whose single-year realizations are dominated by threshold-crossing noise provides an unstable foundation for climatological analysis regardless of the aggregation period applied. As a lesson learnt, CDD depends on the spatial resolution of the data and, at the kilometre scale, on single precipitation events close to the threshold; CDD should therefore only be compared between data sets of similar resolution and interpreted with caution at individual grid cells or stations, including in drought monitoring, impact assessment, and climate model evaluation. This study reports on the surprising fine-scale spatial patterns and resulting shortcomings of the CDD metric and is therefore submitted as a LESSONS report, a paper category dedicated to documenting Limitations, Errors, Surprises, Shortcomings, and Opportunities for New Science.

articles.title: Multi-year convection-permitting irrigation impacts across the European continent
articles.titleEn: Multi-year convection-permitting irrigation impacts across the European continent
articles.abstract: Irrigation is an important anthropogenic activity that can impact surface and atmospheric conditions. In fact, global, regional and local studies that included irrigation in Earth system models already demonstrated the effects of irrigation in different variables. Some regional and local simulations have studied the irrigation impact in some parts of Europe with simulations limited to the duration of one growing season. However, long-term irrigation simulations that cover the whole European continent are still missing. This study quantifies the long-term impact of irrigation on surface and atmospheric variables over the EURO-CORDEX domain using convection-permitting simulations with the Icosahedral Nonhydrostatic (ICON) model that cover a period of 12 years. Our findings indicate that the magnitude of the irrigation impact is limited by the irrigated region and the climate conditions of a given year in the EURO-CORDEX domain, showing that the land–atmosphere coupling is key to determine the irrigation effects. For instance, the cold and wet summer of 2017 in south Europe weakened the irrigation cooling in the Alps. In contrast, the heat wave of 2018 in Central Europe enabled the influence of irrigation on surface variables in this region. Regarding precipitation, we found no robust climatological precipitation response to irrigation across the 12 year analysis. articles.title: Coupling LaMEM 3.0.1 and FastScape 2.8.4 for self-consistent 3D thermo-mechanical and landscape evolution modeling
articles.titleEn: Coupling LaMEM 3.0.1 and FastScape 2.8.4 for self-consistent 3D thermo-mechanical and landscape evolution modeling
articles.abstract: The feedback between tectonic events and surface processes shapes both landscapes and lithospheric deformation, yet 3D numerical models that couple thermo-mechanical processes with landscape evolution remain uncommon, partly due to mismatches in temporal and spatial scales between the two. Here, we present a coupling module implemented within LaMEM that couples the thermo-mechanical code LaMEM with the landscape evolution code FastScape. The method transfers surface velocities from the parallel LaMEM grid to a persistent FastScape grid, subdivides each thermo-mechanical timestep into landscape evolution substeps, and returns the updated topography to LaMEM for free-surface and material-phase updates. The module supports 2D and 3D LaMEM configurations, as well as both uniform and non-uniform thermo-mechanical grids. Parameter and resolution tests demonstrate stable behaviour across the investigated buoyancy, bedrock erodibility, hillslope diffusivity, and surface grid settings. A comparison between a 2D-coupled and a fully 3D configuration of a plume-induced dome shows that the 3D model captures the dome-shaped uplift and radial drainage. A 3D subduction model with an oceanic plateau demonstrates the module in a large-scale application with along-strike variability. The source code, input files, and a user manual for the presented tests are archived in a persistent public repository.

articles.title: Idealised framework to prescribe sea surface temperatures to investigate the atmospheric circulation response
articles.titleEn: Idealised framework to prescribe sea surface temperatures to investigate the atmospheric circulation response
articles.abstract: Midlatitude sea surface temperature (SST) fronts exert a strong influence on storm tracks and westerly jets by modulating lower-tropospheric baroclinicity, moisture availability, and diabatic heating. Yet the sensitivity of the large-scale atmospheric circulation to the detailed structure of these fronts remains difficult to isolate in realistic model configurations. Here we introduce an idealised SST framework for aquaplanet experiments that allows to prescribe the strength, width, and latitude of a midlatitude SST front. The SST profile is constructed from analytically derived meridional gradients, ensuring that changes to the front generate physically consistent moisture distributions through the Clausius–Clapeyron relation. Using this framework, we conduct a suite of sensitivity experiments to quantify the influence from various aspects in the structure of the SST front on the climatological-mean energy and water cycles as well as the associated atmospheric circulation. Preliminary results demonstrate that increasing the frontal SST gradient or narrowing the frontal width systematically intensifies storm-track activity and strengthens the midlatitude jet, whereas shifting the front meridionally alters the latitudinal position of storm tracks in a non-linear manner. Warm- and cold-climate experiments further show that imposing a fixed freezing threshold in atmosphere-only setups artificially reduces high-latitude baroclinicity, whereas allowing SSTs to go below freezing produces a more realistic polar thermal structure. Overall, our results demonstrate that the experimental framework developed in this study provides a useful basis for targeted process studies of how midlatitude SST-front characteristics shape the atmospheric circulation, energy budget, and hydrological cycle.

articles.title: A new Monte Carlo treatment of multiple scattering of light by black carbon aggregates with varying levels of compactness
articles.titleEn: A new Monte Carlo treatment of multiple scattering of light by black carbon aggregates with varying levels of compactness
articles.abstract: We use a specially designed Monte Carlo (MC) model that includes individual Mueller matrix selection in each scattering event to conduct a comprehensive theoretical investigation of the intensity and polarization of light multiply scattered by an atmospheric layer embedded with black carbon (BC) particles with varying compactness. We find that the spatial distributions of the degree of linear and circular polarization are sensitive to BC particle shape, and that depolarization is more dominant for spherical BC particles than for fractal aggregates. We also find that the layer transmittance is highest for the more spherical BC particle shapes and lowest for the extended fractal aggregates, with an overall difference of approximately 10 % relative to the incident intensity between the highest and lowest values of transmittance. We find that the reflectance exhibits a similar tendency, and that correspondingly, the layer absorptance is lowest for the more spherical BC shapes and highest for the extended fractal aggregates. In addition, we compare the results obtained from our MC simulations with those obtained with the delta-Eddington approximation for the same optical thickness, single scattering albedo, asymmetry factor, and incident zenith angle. We find that there is a relatively small difference between our results and the delta-Eddington results with respect to the layer transmittance and the layer absorbance, but that the layer reflectance obtained with our MC simulations is up to 50 % lower than that obtained with the delta-Eddington approximation. These results could have important implications for radiative forcing estimations, climate modeling, and remote sensing implementations.

articles.title: Drivers of reduced permafrost cooling efficacy of equatorial stratospheric aerosol injection in the Eastern Arctic compared to a moderate emission pathway
articles.titleEn: Drivers of reduced permafrost cooling efficacy of equatorial stratospheric aerosol injection in the Eastern Arctic compared to a moderate emission pathway
articles.abstract: The Arctic is warming about four times faster than the global average, with permafrost thaw representing a potential global climate tipping element. Given the insufficient rate of carbon emission reductions, stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) has emerged as a strategy to abate climate warming. However, its effects on permafrost thaw drivers remain uncertain. The G6sulfur and G6solar experiments, part of the Geoengineering Model Intercomparison Project (GeoMIP6), aim to offset the warming in the high-emission scenario (ssp585) to achieve global-mean near-surface air temperatures comparable to those in the moderate-emission scenario (ssp245), through the injection of stratospheric aerosols near the equator (G6sulfur) or a reduction in top-of-atmosphere solar irradiance (G6solar), respectively. Analyzing both experiments, we find that G6sulfur alters atmospheric circulation, modifying winds, cloud properties, and the North Atlantic Oscillation, which affect temperature patterns and longwave radiation. These changes shift the relative importance of mechanisms driving summer permafrost thaw, resulting in a robust east–west dipole in thaw depth (+0.769 m, 6/6 models): increased thaw in the Eastern Hemisphere (+0.491 m) and a significant but less model-consistent reduction in thaw in the Western Hemisphere (−0.278 m), compared to the ssp245 scenario targeted by the intervention. While both G6sulfur and G6solar slow permafrost decline by 2080–2099 relative to ssp585 (+4.61 × 10 6 and +5.37 × 10 6 km 2 respectively), neither preserves as much permafrost area as ssp245 (−1.08 × 10 6 km 2 for G6sulfur and −0.32 × 10 6 km 2 for G6solar). By altering the drivers of permafrost dynamics, G6sulfur creates spatial variations in thaw patterns, resulting in an overall reduction in permafrost area compared to ssp245. Our findings underscore the need to better understand and optimize SAI deployment to avoid unintended regional impacts.
